Partial regularity for a surface growth model

Wojciech S. Ożański    James C. Robinson
Abstract

We prove two partial regularity results for the scalar equation ut+ux​x​x​x+∂x​xux2=0u_{t}+u_{xxxx}+\partial_{xx}u_{x}^{2}=0, a model of surface growth arising from the physical process of molecular epitaxy. We show that the set of space-time singularities has (upper) box-counting dimension no larger than 7/67/6 and 11-dimensional (parabolic) Hausdorff measure zero. These parallel the results available for the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations. In fact the mathematical theory of the surface growth model is known to share a number of striking similarities with the Navier–Stokes equations, and the partial regularity results are the next step towards understanding this remarkable similarity. As far as we know the surface growth model is the only lower-dimensional “mini-model” of the Navier–Stokes equations for which such an analogue of the partial regularity theory has been proved. In the course of our proof, which is inspired by the rescaling analysis of Lin (1998) and Ladyzhenskaya & Seregin (1999), we develop certain nonlinear parabolic Poincaré inequality, which is a concept of independent interest. We believe that similar inequalities could be applicable in other parabolic equations.

1 Introduction

In this paper we consider the one-dimensional model of surface growth

ut+ux​x​x​x+∂x​xux2=0u_{t}+u_{xxxx}+\partial_{xx}u_{x}^{2}=0 (1.1)

on the one-dimensional torus 𝕋{\mathbb{T}}, under the assumption that ∫𝕋u=0\int_{{\mathbb{T}}}u=0; we refer to this in what follows as the SGM.

As previously observed by Blömker & Romito [2, 3], this model shares many striking similarities with the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations. In particular, in their 2009 paper Blömker & Romito proved local existence in the critical space H˙1/2\dot{H}^{1/2} and (spatial) smoothness for solutions bounded in L8/(2​α−1)​((0,T),Hα)L^{8/(2\alpha-1)}((0,T);H^{\alpha}) for all 1/2<α<9/21/2<\alpha<9/2; in the 2012 paper they prove local existence in a critical space of a similar type to that occurring in the paper by Koch & Tataru [10] for the Navier–Stokes equations.

The aim of this paper is to prove partial regularity results for (1.1) that are analogues of those proved by Caffarelli, Kohn, & Nirenberg [4] for the Navier–Stokes equations. Perhaps surprisingly their inductive method does not seem well adapted to (1.1), and instead we use the rescaling approach of Lin [14] and Ladyzhenskaya & Seregin [12]. The main issue is that the biharmonic heat kernel, given in the one-dimensional case by

K(x,t)=αt−1/4f(|x|t−1/4),wheref(x)=∫0∞e−s4cos(xs)dsK(x,t)=\alpha t^{-1/4}f(|x|t^{-1/4}),\qquad\mbox{where}\qquad f(x)=\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm e}^{-s^{4}}\cos(xs)\,{\rm d}s

and α\alpha is a normalising constant, takes negative values so cannot be used as the basis of the construction of a suitable sequence of test functions for use in the local energy inequality.

Our main result is the following.

Theorem 1.1.

Let uu be a suitable weak solution of the surface growth model. Then

  1. (i)

    there exist ε0,R0>0\varepsilon_{0},R_{0}>0 such that if r<R0r<R_{0} and

    1r2​∫Q⁡(z,r)|ux|3≤ε0\frac{1}{r^{2}}\int_{Q(z,r)}|u_{x}|^{3}\leq\varepsilon_{0}

    for a cylinder Q⁡(z,r)Q(z,r), then uu is Hölder continuous in Q⁡(z,r/2)Q(z,r/2);

  2. (ii)

    there exists ε1>0\varepsilon_{1}>0 such that if either

    lim supr→01r​∫Q⁡(z,r)ux​x2≤ε1 or lim supr→0{supt−r4≤s≤t+r41r​∫Br​(x)u​(s)2}≤ε1\limsup_{r\to 0}\frac{1}{r}\int_{Q(z,r)}u_{xx}^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{1}\quad\text{ or }\quad\limsup_{r\to 0}\left\{\sup_{t-r^{4}\leq s\leq t+r^{4}}\frac{1}{r}\int_{B_{r}(x)}u(s)^{2}\right\}\leq\varepsilon_{1}

    then uu is Hölder continuous in Q⁡(z,ρ)Q(z,\rho) for some ρ>0\rho>0.

Here Q⁡(z,r)Q(z,r) denotes the parabolic cylinder of radius rr centred at zz (see Section 1.1 below), and the notion (and existence) of suitable weak solutions is discussed in Section 2. Using these conditional regularity results we deduce upper bounds on the dimension of the space-time singular set, which we take here to be

S={(x,t)∈𝕋×(0,∞):u is not space-time Hölder continuousin any neighbourhood of (x,t)}.\begin{split}S&=\{(x,t)\in{\mathbb{T}}\times(0,\infty):\ u\mbox{ is not space-time H\"{o}lder continuous}\\ &\hskip 128.0374pt\qquad\qquad\qquad\mbox{in any neighbourhood of }(x,t)\}.\end{split} (1.2)

Note that SS is closed. Namely we show that for every compact K⊂𝕋×(0,∞)K\subset\mathbb{T}\times(0,\infty)

dB​(S∩K)≤7/6 and 𝒫1​(S)=0,d_{B}(S\cap K)\leq 7/6\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathcal{P}^{1}(S)=0,

see Corollary 4.6 and Corollary 5.4, respectively. Here dBd_{B} denotes the (upper) box-counting dimension (see (4.17) for the definition) and 𝒫1\mathcal{P}^{1} denotes the 11-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure appropriate for scaling of the equations (see (5.10) for details). The point of considering the intersection S∩KS\cap K is to separate SS from the set {(x,0):x∈𝕋}\{(x,0)\colon x\in\mathbb{T}\}. This is a technical matter related to the definition of the box-counting dimension. Indeed, in order to deduce the bound from part (i) of the theorem above one first needs to guarantee that Q⁡(z,r)⊂𝕋×(0,∞)Q(z,r)\subset\mathbb{T}\times(0,\infty) for sufficiently small rr, uniformly in z∈Sz\in S (see the proof of Corollary 4.6), and we overcome this problem by intersecting SS with a compact set. (A similar issue appears in the case of the Navier–Stokes equations, see Theorem 15.8 in Robinson et al. [18].) This issue does not appear in the second estimate, 𝒫1​(S)=0\mathcal{P}^{1}(S)=0, and in the case when the initial condition of a suitable weak solution is sufficiently regular (say H1/2H^{1/2}) as then a weak-strong uniqueness result (see Theorem 2.11 in Blömker & Romito [2], for example) guarantees that uu is smooth for small times.

The estimate 𝒫1​(S)=0\mathcal{P}^{1}(S)=0 implies that dH​(S)d_{H}(S), the Hausdorff dimension of SS, is no greater than 11. In the case of the Navier–Stokes equations, the corresponding results are dB​(S∩K)≤5/3d_{B}(S\cap K)\leq 5/3 for any compact set KK and 𝒫N​S​E1​(S)=0\mathcal{P}^{1}_{NSE}(S)=0 (see, for example, Chapters 15 and 16 in [18]), where 𝒫N​S​E1\mathcal{P}^{1}_{NSE} is the 11-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure which respects the Navier–Stokes scaling in ℝ3×ℝ\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{R} (hence the subscript “NSE”). In the case of the Navier–Stokes equations the bound on the box-counting dimension has been improved, the current sharpest bound being dB​(S∩K)≤2400/1903(≈1.261)d_{B}(S\cap K)\leq 2400/1903(\approx 1.261), due to He et al. [8].

As for the definition (1.2), note that if uu is spatially Hölder continuous on 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} with some exponent θ\theta then u∈Hα​(𝕋)u\in H^{\alpha}({\mathbb{T}}) for all 0<α<θ0<\alpha<\theta, using the Sobolev–Slobodeckii characterisation of Hα​(𝕋)H^{\alpha}({\mathbb{T}}) as the collection of all functions such that

∫𝕋∫𝕋|f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)|2|x−y|1+2​α​𝑑x​𝑑y<∞\int_{\mathbb{T}}\int_{\mathbb{T}}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|^{2}}{|x-y|^{1+2\alpha}}\,{\rm d}x\,{\rm d}y<\infty

(see Di Nezza, Palatucci, & Valdinoci [5]); it follows (using arguments from Blömker & Romito [2]) that if uu is space-time Hölder continuous on [0,T]×𝕋[0,T]\times{\mathbb{T}} then uu is spatially smooth. However, the condition u∈Lt∞​Lx∞u\in L^{\infty}_{t}L^{\infty}_{x} (which is the SGM equivalent of the Lt∞​Lx3L^{\infty}_{t}L^{3}_{x} regularity for the Navier–Stokes equations, see Escauriaza, Seregin, & Sv̌erák [6]) is not yet known to be sufficient for the regularity of the SGM. This is why we do not use local essential boundedness in our definition of SS. Observe also that SS is closed (as its complement is open in 𝕋×(0,∞)\mathbb{T}\times(0,\infty)).

Note that it is not entirely clear whether or not the definition in (1.2) is the correct one for the SGM, since a local conditional regularity result that guarantees spatial smoothness under a localised Hölder condition of uu is currently unknown. However, a closely related result has recently been proved by Ożański [16]: if ux∈Ltq′​Lxq​(Q)u_{x}\in L_{t}^{q^{\prime}}L_{x}^{q}(Q), where QQ is a cylinder and q′,q∈(1,∞]q^{\prime},q\in(1,\infty] are such that 4/q′+1/q≤14/q^{\prime}+1/q\leq 1, then u∈C∞​(Q)u\in C^{\infty}(Q). This can be thought of as an analogue of the local Serrin condition in the Navier–Stokes equation, which guarantees that a weak solution uu satisfying u∈Ltq′​Lxq​(Q)u\in L_{t}^{q^{\prime}}L_{x}^{q}(Q) for 2/q′+3/q=12/q^{\prime}+3/q=1 is smooth in space, see Section 8.5 in Robinson et al. [18], for example.

The structure of the article is as follows. In the remainder of this section we introduce some notation, in Section 2 we introduce the notion of suitable weak solutions and we show global-in-time existence of such solutions for any initial condition u0∈L2u_{0}\in L^{2} with zero mean. In Section 3 we introduce a “nonlinear parabolic Poincaré inequality”, which is vital for both of our partial regularity results and a concept of independent interest. We then prove two local regularity results for the surface growth model, the first in terms of uxu_{x} (Section 4) and the second one in terms of ux​xu_{xx} (Section 5). As a consequence we can show that the (upper) box-counting dimension of the space-time singular set is no larger than 7/67/6, and that its one-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure is zero.

2 Suitable weak solutions

We first define the notion of a weak solution of the problem (1.1).

The limit function uu is a weak solution to the surface growth initial value problem since the regularity requirement (2.2) follows from the convergence above and (2.3) follows by taking the limit τn→0+\tau_{n}\to 0^{+} in (2.10) after integration by parts in time of the left-hand side.∎

As with the partial regularity theory for the Navier–Stokes equations, we make key use of a local energy inequality. This gives rise to the notion of “suitable weak solutions”, which we now define.

Definition 2.3 (Suitable weak solution).

We say that a weak solution is suitable if the local energy inequality

12​∫u​(t)2​ϕ​(t)+∫0t∫ux​x2​ϕ≤∫0t∫(12​(ϕt−ϕx​x​x​x)​u2CLOSEOPEN+2​ux2​ϕx​x−53​ux3​ϕx−ux2​u​ϕx​x)\begin{split}\frac{1}{2}\int u(t)^{2}\phi(t)+\int_{0}^{t}\int u_{xx}^{2}\phi&\leq\int_{0}^{t}\int\left(\frac{1}{2}(\phi_{t}-\phi_{xxxx})u^{2}\right.\\ &\hskip 56.9055pt\left.+2u_{x}^{2}\phi_{xx}-\frac{5}{3}u_{x}^{3}\phi_{x}-u_{x}^{2}u\phi_{xx}\right)\end{split} (2.12)

u⁡(ut+ux​x​x​x+∂x​xux2)≤0;u\left(u_{t}+u_{xxxx}+\partial_{xx}u_{x}^{2}\right)\leq 0;

By adapting the method outlined above in the proof of the existence of a weak solution, we now show that this solution also satisfies the local energy inequality and is therefore ‘suitable’.

3 A ‘nonlinear’ parabolic Poincaré inequality

Here we prove a parabolic version of the Poincaré inequality, which is a key ingredient in the proof of the partial regularity results that follow.

Theorem 3.1 (Parabolic Poincaré inequality).

Let η∈[0,1]\eta\in[0,1], r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) and let Q⁡(z0,r)Q(z_{0},r) be a cylinder, where z0=(x0,t0)z_{0}=(x_{0},t_{0}). If a function uu satisfies

∫Br​(x0)(u⁡(t)−u⁡(s))​ϕ=∫st∫Br​(x0)ux​ϕx​x​x−η​∫st∫Br​(x0)ux2​ϕx​x\int_{B_{r}(x_{0})}(u(t)-u(s))\phi=\int_{s}^{t}\int_{B_{r}(x_{0})}u_{x}\phi_{xxx}-\eta\int_{s}^{t}\int_{B_{r}(x_{0})}u_{x}^{2}\phi_{xx} (3.1)

for all ϕ∈C0∞​(Br​(x0))\phi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(B_{r}(x_{0})) and almost every s,t∈(−r4,r4)s,t\in(-r^{4},r^{4}) with s<ts<t, then

1r5​∫Q⁡(z0,r/2)|u−uz0,r/2|3≤cp​p​(Y⁡(z0,r)+η​Y​(z0,r)2),\frac{1}{r^{5}}\int_{Q(z_{0},r/2)}|u-u_{z_{0},r/2}|^{3}\leq c_{pp}\left({\rm Y}(z_{0},r)+\eta{\rm Y}(z_{0},r)^{2}\right), (3.2)

where

Y⁡(z0,r):=1r2​∫Q⁡(z0,r)|ux|3{\rm Y}(z_{0},r):=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\int_{Q(z_{0},r)}|u_{x}|^{3} (3.3)

and cp​p>0c_{pp}>0 is an absolute constant.

Recall uz0,r/2u_{z_{0},r/2} denotes the mean of uu over Q⁡(z0,r/2)Q(z_{0},r/2) (see (1.3)). Note that no tt derivative appears on the right-hand side of (3.2). Observe that (3.2) is the classical Poincaré inequality if η=0\eta=0 and the left-hand side is replaced by

1r5​∫Q⁡(z0,r/2)|u−⨏B⁡(x0,r/2)u⁡(t)|​𝑑x​𝑑t\frac{1}{r^{5}}\int_{Q(z_{0},r/2)}\left|u-\fint_{B(x_{0},r/2)}u(t)\right|\,{\rm d}x\,{\rm d}t

(i.e. the mean over the cylinder is replaced by the mean over the ball at each time). Moreover note that (3.2) does not hold for arbitrary functions since adding a function of time to uu allows one to increase the left-hand side while keeping the right-hand side bounded. This also verifies the relevance of the assumption (3.1) since it shows that the only function of time which can be added to uu is a constant function. On the other hand, adding constants to uu makes no change to (3.2).

Furthermore, the case η=0\eta=0 gives the parabolic Poincaré inequality for weak solutions to the biharmonic heat equation:

1r3​∫Q⁡(z0,r/2)|u−uz0,r/2|3≤cp​p​∫Q⁡(z0,r)|ux|3,\frac{1}{r^{3}}\int_{Q(z_{0},r/2)}|u-u_{z_{0},r/2}|^{3}\leq c_{pp}\int_{Q(z_{0},r)}|u_{x}|^{3},

whenever ut=∂x4uu_{t}=\partial_{x}^{4}u (weakly). In this case it can be shown that the inequality holds in any dimension (with ∂x4\partial_{x}^{4} replaced by the bilaplacian Δ2\Delta^{2}) and for any p≥1p\geq 1.

Due to (2.4) any weak solution of the surface growth equation satisfies (3.1) for all z0z_{0}, rr as long as Q⁡(z0,r)⊂𝕋×(0,T)Q(z_{0},r)\subset\mathbb{T}\times(0,T), and hence we can use inequality (3.2) for the suitable weak solutions that form our main subject in what follows.

4 The first conditional and partial regularity results

Here we show local regularity of suitable weak solutions to the surface growth equation based on a condition on uxu_{x}. Namely, we will show in Theorem 4.5 that there exists ε0>0\varepsilon_{0}>0 and R0>0R_{0}>0 such that if

1r2​∫Q⁡(z,r)|ux|3<ε0\frac{1}{r^{2}}\int_{Q(z,r)}|u_{x}|^{3}<\varepsilon_{0}

for some r<R0r<R_{0} and zz then uu is Hölder continuous in Q⁡(z,r/2)Q(z,r/2).

The proof we give of this result is based on that presented for the Navier–Stokes equations by Ladyzhenskaya & Seregin [12]; we begin with a certain ‘one-step’ decay estimate, which we then iterate.

4.1 Interior regularity for the biharmonic heat flow

The proof of the decay estimate relies on the following regularity result for the biharmonic heat equation; while the result is perhaps ‘standard’, we could not find an obvious canonical reference, and so for the sake of completeness we provide a short proof.

‖vx‖L∞​(Qb)≤Ca,b​(‖v‖L2​(Qa)+‖vx‖L2​(Qa))\|v_{x}\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{b})}\leq C_{a,b}\left(\|v\|_{L^{2}(Q_{a})}+\|v_{x}\|_{L^{2}(Q_{a})}\right)

Blömker & Romito [2] showed that if

Since H1​(𝕋)⊂L∞​(𝕋)H^{1}({\mathbb{T}})\subset L^{\infty}({\mathbb{T}}), it follows in particular that if

Using Theorem 5.2 we can obtain improved bounds on the dimension of the singular set in terms of the (parabolic) Hausdorff measure. For a set X⊂ℝ×ℝX\subset{\mathbb{R}}\times{\mathbb{R}} and k≥0k\geq 0 let

Pk​(X):=limδ→0+Pδk​(X)P^{k}(X):=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0^{+}}P_{\delta}^{k}(X) (5.10)

denote the kk-dimensional parabolic Hausdorff measure, where

Pδk(X):=inf{∑i=1∞rik:X⊂⋃iQri:ri<δ},P_{\delta}^{k}(X):=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}r_{i}^{k}:\ X\subset\bigcup_{i}Q_{r_{i}}:\ r_{i}<\delta\right\},

and Qri=Qri​(x,t)Q_{r_{i}}=Q_{r_{i}}(x,t) is a rir_{i}-cylinder, i≥1i\geq 1. Observe that P1​(X)=0P^{1}(X)=0 if and only if for every δ>0\delta>0 the set XX can be covered by a collection {Qri}\{Q_{r_{i}}\} such that ∑iri<δ\sum_{i}r_{i}<\delta.

Corollary 5.4 (Partial regularity II).

The singular set SS of a suitable weak solution of (1.1) satisfies 𝒫1​(S)=0\mathcal{P}^{1}(S)=0.

Note that this in particular gives dH​(S)≤1d_{H}(S)\leq 1 (since ℋ1​(S)≤c​𝒫1​(S)\mathcal{H}^{1}(S)\leq c\mathcal{P}^{1}(S), where ℋ1\mathcal{H}^{1} denotes the 11-dimensional Hausdorff measure).

We will need the Vitali Covering Lemma in the following form: given a family of parabolic cylinders Qr​(x,t)Q_{r}(x,t), there exists a countable (or finite) disjoint subfamily {Qri​(xi,ti)}\{Q_{r_{i}}(x_{i},t_{i})\} such that for any cylinder Qr​(x,t)Q_{r}(x,t) in the original family there exists an ii such that Qr​(x,t)⊂Q5​ri​(xi,ti)Q_{r}(x,t)\subset Q_{5r_{i}}(x_{i},t_{i}). (For a proof see Caffarelli, Kohn & Nirenberg (1982).)

Proof.

Fix δ>0\delta>0 and let VV be an open set containing SS such that

5ε1​∫Vux​x2≤δ.\frac{5}{\varepsilon_{1}}\int_{V}u_{xx}^{2}\leq\delta.

Such VV exists since ux​x∈L2​(𝕋×(0,T))u_{xx}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{T}\times(0,T)) (recall (2.2)) and since |S|=0|S|=0 (see the comments preceding this section). For each (x,t)∈S(x,t)\in S, choose r∈(0,δ)r\in(0,\delta) such that Qr/5​(x,t)⊂VQ_{r/5}(x,t)\subset V and

5r​∫Qr/5​(x,t)ux​x2>ε1.\frac{5}{r}\int_{Q_{r/5}(x,t)}u_{xx}^{2}>\varepsilon_{1}.

Such a choice is possible, for otherwise the point (x,t)(x,t) would be regular due to Theorem 5.2. We now use the Vitali Covering Lemma to extract a countable (or finite) disjoint subcollection of these cylinders {Qri/5​(xi,ti)}\{Q_{r_{i}/5}(x_{i},t_{i})\} such that the singular set SS is still covered by {Qri​(xi,ti)}\{Q_{r_{i}}(x_{i},t_{i})\}. Then

∑iri≤5ε1​∑i∫Qri/5​(xi,ti)ux​x2≤5ε1​∫Vux​x2≤δ,\sum_{i}r_{i}\leq\frac{5}{\varepsilon_{1}}\sum_{i}\int_{Q_{r_{i}/5}(x_{i},t_{i})}u_{xx}^{2}\leq\frac{5}{\varepsilon_{1}}\int_{V}u_{xx}^{2}\leq\delta,

as required. ∎

6 Conclusion and further discussion

We have proved two conditional regularity results, and as a consequence two bounds on singular space-time set for the SGM:

dB​(S∩K)≤7/6andP1​(S)=0,d_{B}(S\cap K)\leq 7/6\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad P^{1}(S)=0,

for any compact K⊂𝕋×(0,∞)K\subset\mathbb{T}\times(0,\infty). As with the Navier–Stokes equations, there is a gap here between the box-counting and Hausdorff dimensions; as with the NSE, it is an open question whether these dimension estimates can be equalised.

In this context, it would be interesting to adapt the constructions due to Scheffer [21, 22], see also Ożański [15, 17]) of solutions of the weak form of the ‘Navier–Stokes inequality’ that have a space-time singular set of Hausdorff dimension γ\gamma for any γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) to the SGM. This seems difficult, since the constructions make use of (i) the three-dimensional nature of the fluid flow and (ii) the pressure function plays a fundamental role in amplifying the magnitude of the velocity.

There are some outstanding conditional regularity problems for the SGM: one is to prove a local version of the L8/(2​α−1)​(0,T,Hα)L^{8/(2\alpha-1)}(0,T;H^{\alpha}) regularity condition (this result is only known in a global form, see introduction); and the other to prove the same for u∈Lt∞​Lx∞u\in L^{\infty}_{t}L^{\infty}_{x}, both globally and locally. In particular the first would imply that the complement of our ‘singular set’ SS really does consist of points in a neighbourhood of which uu is regular in space.

|fz,r/2−fz,r|≤4n​(⨏Qr​(z)|f⁡(y)−fz,r|p​𝑑t)1/p≤4n​M​rβ.|f_{z,r/2}-f_{z,r}|\leq 4^{n}\left(\fint_{Q_{r}(z)}|f(y)-f_{z,r}|^{p}\,{\rm d}t\right)^{1/p}\leq 4^{n}Mr^{\beta}.

Now consider fz,2−k−fz,rf_{z,2^{-k}}-f_{z,r}. Since

fz,r​2−k−fz,r=∑j=1kfz,r​2−k−fz,r​2−(k−1),f_{z,r2^{-k}}-f_{z,r}=\sum_{j=1}^{k}f_{z,r2^{-k}}-f_{z,r2^{-(k-1)}},

it follows that

|fz,r​2−k−fz,r|≤∑j=1kc​M​rβ​2−(j−1)​β≤∑j=0∞c​M​rβ​2−j​β=c​M​rβ.\left|f_{z,r2^{-k}}-f_{z,r}\right|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{k}cMr^{\beta}2^{-(j-1)\beta}\leq\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}cMr^{\beta}2^{-j\beta}=cMr^{\beta}. (A.4)

This shows that fz,r​2−kf_{z,r2^{-k}} forms a Cauchy sequence, and hence the averages converge for every z∈Qr/2​(0)z\in Q_{r/2}(0). By the Lebesgue Differentiation Theorem, these averages converge to f⁡(z)f(z) for almost every zz, and so if we let k→∞k\rightarrow\infty in (A.4) we obtain an estimate for the difference between f⁡(z)f(z) and its average,

|f⁡(z)−fz,r|≤c1​M​rβ.|f(z)-f_{z,r}|\leq c_{1}Mr^{\beta}.

Now take another point ζ∈QR/2​(0)\zeta\in Q_{R/2}(0); we compare fz,rf_{z,r} with fζ,2​rf_{\zeta,2r}:

|fz,r−fζ,2​r|p\displaystyle|f_{z,r}-f_{\zeta,2r}|^{p} =|1rn​V​∫Qr​(z)f⁡(y)−fζ,2​r​𝑑y|p\displaystyle=\left|\frac{1}{r^{n}V}\int_{Q_{r}(z)}f(y)-f_{\zeta,2r}\,{\rm d}y\right|^{p}
≤1rn​V​∫Qr​(z)|f⁡(y)−fζ,2​r|p​𝑑y,\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{r^{n}V}\int_{Q_{r}(z)}|f(y)-f_{\zeta,2r}|^{p}\,{\rm d}y,

arguing as before. Now if z=(x,t)z=(x,t) and ζ=(ξ,s)\zeta=(\xi,s), choose

r=|x−ξ|+|t−s|1/α;r=|x-\xi|+|t-s|^{1/\alpha};

then Qr​(x,t)⊂Q2​r​(ξ,s)Q_{r}(x,t)\subset Q_{2r}(\xi,s), and so we can enlarge the domain of integration to obtain

|fz,r−fζ,2​r|p\displaystyle|f_{z,r}-f_{\zeta,2r}|^{p} ≤2n(2​r)n​V​∫Q2​r​(ζ)|f⁡(y)−fζ,2​r|p​𝑑y\displaystyle\leq\frac{2^{n}}{(2r)^{n}V}\int_{Q_{2r}(\zeta)}|f(y)-f_{\zeta,2r}|^{p}\,{\rm d}y
=2n​⨏Q2​r​(ζ)|f⁡(y)−fζ,2​r|p​𝑑y\displaystyle=2^{n}\fint_{Q_{2r}(\zeta)}|f(y)-f_{\zeta,2r}|^{p}\,{\rm d}y
≤2n​Mp​(2​r)p​β,\displaystyle\leq 2^{n}M^{p}(2r)^{p\beta},

i.e.

|fz,r−fζ,2​r|≤2p+(n/p)​M​rβ.|f_{z,r}-f_{\zeta,2r}|\leq 2^{p+(n/p)}Mr^{\beta}.

So now (still with rr chosen as above)

|f⁡(z)−f⁡(ζ)|\displaystyle|f(z)-f(\zeta)| ≤|f⁡(z)−fz,r|+|fz,r−fζ,2​r|+|fζ,2​r−f⁡(ζ)|\displaystyle\leq|f(z)-f_{z,r}|+|f_{z,r}-f_{\zeta,2r}|+|f_{\zeta,2r}-f(\zeta)|
≤c1​M​rβ+c2​M​rβ+c1​M​(2​r)β\displaystyle\leq c_{1}Mr^{\beta}+c_{2}Mr^{\beta}+c_{1}M(2r)^{\beta}
=c​M​(|x−y|+|t−s|1/α)β,\displaystyle=cM(|x-y|+|t-s|^{1/\alpha})^{\beta},

which is (A.3). ∎
